The POST handler can obtain its input from a client-controlled cookie (lines 39 and 46), and hashes it with SHA-1 before storing the digest in a file (lines 63–68). Since this is explicitly storing a sensitive value as a password-like hash, SHA-1 is an unsuitable weak, fast hash for security-sensitive storage.

The handler takes an attacker-controlled cookie value (lines 39–50), hashes it directly with unsalted SHA-1 (lines 60–63), then persists the digest as a “hash_value” (lines 64–65). Thus the evaluated expression is confined to one single-quoted string literal; backslash escapes may alter its string value but cannot introduce executable syntax outside that literal. The POST handler takes a cookie value, URL-decodes it, stores it as a ConfigParser option, then retrieves that same value and executes it at line 51. An attacker controlling the cookie can supply Python code, so this is remotely reachable arbitrary code execution.

The POST handler takes a client-controlled cookie, URL-decodes it, and passes it through `thing.doSomething` to `bar`; the check only ensures `bar` is surrounded by quotes and has no interior single quote. Because clients can supply or alter cookies, an attacker can provide a pickle payload and trigger unsafe deserialization; the hardcoded cookie set by the GET handler does not constrain the POST input.
